meta.title: Who really said "If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Goldman never said it. The sentence was composed for a 1973 T-shirt from a passage in her memoir — the feeling is hers, the words are not.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If I can't dance, I don't want to be part of your revolution'?
meta.ogDescription: Emma Goldman never wrote this. It was composed for a T-shirt in 1973, out of a real passage in Living My Life about being told not to dance.

answer.label: Emma Goldman — but not in these words
answer.sourceLine: The sentiment is hers and comes from a real incident she describes in Living My Life (1931): told that it “did not behoove an agitator to dance”, she refused to accept that her cause required the denial of joy. But she never compressed it into this sentence. Wikipedia records ↗ that the wording was composed by a printer in 1973 for a T-shirt.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Emma Goldman, describing an incident from her early years in New York
Composed in 1973 by a printer, for a T-shirt
Alix Kates Shulman sent him the passage; he condensed it into a sentence

source.excerpt: At the dances I was one of the most untiring and gayest. One evening a cousin of Sasha, a young boy, took me aside. With a grave face, as if he were about to announce the death of a dear comrade, he whispered to me that it did not behoove an agitator to dance. … I told him to mind his own business. I was tired of having the Cause constantly thrown into my face. I did not believe that a Cause which stood for a beautiful ideal, for anarchism, for release and freedom from convention and prejudice, should demand the denial of life and joy. I insisted that our Cause could not expect me to become a nun and that the movement would not be turned into a cloister. If it meant that, I did not want it. “I want freedom, the right to self-expression, everybody’s right to beautiful, radiant things.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ prints the Living My Life passage in its sourced section and appends a note that this incident “was the source of a statement commonly attributed to Goldman that occurs in several variants” — then lists them, including this one word for word.

Wikipedia ↗ gives the mechanism: in 1973 the feminist writer Alix Kates Shulman was asked by a printer friend for a Goldman quotation to put on a T-shirt, and sent him this selection. “The printer created a statement based on these sentiments that has become one of the most famous quotations attributed to Goldman even though she probably never said or wrote it as such.”
Wikipedia cites Shulman’s own account, “Dances with Feminists” (Women’s Review of Books, December 1991), and Alice Wexler’s 1989 biography for the T-shirt story and its spread.
source.excerptNote: This is the passage everything descends from, as transcribed in Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗. Note what is not in it: any sentence beginning “if I can’t dance”.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status for the quoted sentence, because nobody can point to the publication it comes from: it was composed for a T-shirt in 1973 by a printer whom the sources do not name. The passage it was built from, in Living My Life, was published in 1931 and is not public domain in the United States.

author.name: Emma Goldman
author.heading: About Emma Goldman
author.bio: Emma Goldman emigrated from Russia to the United States at sixteen and became the most notorious anarchist in the country — imprisoned for urging the unemployed to take bread, for distributing birth-control information, and for opposing conscription in 1917, after which she was deported. She wrote and lectured on free speech, women’s independence and the failure of prisons. Her autobiography Living My Life appeared in 1931.

cite.sourceCitation: Emma Goldman, Living My Life (New York: Alfred A. Knopf, 1931), 56, for the passage the slogan was made from. For the slogan itself: Alix Kates Shulman, “Dances with Feminists,” Women’s Review of Books 9, no. 3 (December 1991), as cited in Wikipedia, which records that the wording was composed by a printer in 1973. No publication by Goldman contains the sentence.

copyAttribution: "If I can’t dance, I don’t want to be part of your revolution." — Attributed to Emma Goldman, but not her words. The sentence was composed by a printer in 1973 for a T-shirt, from a passage Alix Kates Shulman sent him from Goldman’s Living My Life (1931), p. 56, in which Goldman refuses the idea that "a Cause which stood for a beautiful ideal ... should demand the denial of life and joy." The idea is Goldman’s; the wording is not, and it circulates in at least five variants.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is the rare case where the famous person is the right person and the famous sentence is still not theirs. Goldman is on the posters for a reason — she really did refuse to give up dancing for the revolution — but she never put it like this.

items.why: No such line appears in her writings or recorded speeches. Wikipedia states ↗ she “probably never said or wrote it as such”; the wording was a printer’s condensation in 1973.
The underlying refusal is entirely documented, in her own memoir: “I did not believe that a Cause which stood for a beautiful ideal … should demand the denial of life and joy.”

Because no original exists, the wording never settled. Wikiquote lists five ↗, among them “if I can’t dance, it’s not my revolution” and “a revolution without dancing is not a revolution worth having”.

misattribution.truthLine: Yes and no: Goldman is the author of the idea ↗, and an unnamed printer is the author of the sentence.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The incident is small and the stakes were not: a young comrade told Goldman that dancing was undignified in an agitator, and she decided on the spot that a movement demanding that much self-denial was not one she wanted. It is the most human moment in a memoir otherwise full of prisons and deportation.

Forty-two years later the women’s movement rediscovered her, and needed the moment in a form that would fit across a chest. What it got was a sentence Goldman never wrote, carrying an argument she spent her life making — which is why the misattribution has proved impossible to kill.
detailsBody: Shulman had edited Red Emma Speaks (1972) and helped bring Goldman back into print; the T-shirt request came out of that revival. Her own account of what followed, “Dances with Feminists”, appeared in the Women’s Review of Books in December 1991.
Variations have since appeared on thousands of shirts, buttons, posters and mugs — which is a fair definition of a quotation that has escaped its source.
context.pull: The idea is hers. The sentence belongs to a printer nobody named.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote prints the Living My Life p. 56 passage and notes that this incident was the source of a statement commonly attributed to Goldman, listing “If I can’t dance, I don’t want to be part of your revolution” among the variants.

Wikipedia states that in 1973 Alix Kates Shulman sent a printer friend the Living My Life selection, that the printer created the statement from those sentiments, and that Goldman “probably never said or wrote it as such”.
